title: Wedding Hangover Kit: What to Pack for Guests and the Couple
excerpt: What to put in a wedding hangover kit for favors, welcome bags, and bathroom baskets, what to leave out, how to label painkillers safely, and rough budgets.
metaDescription: What to pack in a wedding hangover kit for favors and welcome bags, what to leave out, how to label painkillers safely, and budgets from $2 a kit.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**What goes in a wedding hangover kit:** a small bottle of water, one or two electrolyte packets, a salty snack, something gentle for breakfast, ginger chews or mints, and a note card. Those cover the real problems of the morning after a wedding: dehydration, an unsettled stomach, and an early start for brunch or a flight home. A sealed single-dose painkiller packet is optional, and if you include one it needs a clear alcohol note. Supplements like DHM (dihydromyricetin) are an optional extra at most. Everything else (the cute bag, the pun on the label, the tiny bottle of aspirin with your monogram) is presentation.

A wedding kit is different from an ordinary hangover kit for one reason: you're handing it to a hundred or more people you can't screen. Your guests range from your college roommates to your 80-year-old great-aunt, and they include people who are pregnant, people who don't drink, people on blood thinners or antidepressants, and possibly teenagers. That changes what's smart to put inside. This guide covers how to use hangover kits as wedding favors, welcome bags, and bathroom baskets, what to pack and what to leave out, how to word the card, rough budgets, and the couple's own kit for the day after.

> **This is not medical advice.** A hangover kit can make a rough morning more comfortable. It can't make heavy drinking safe, and nothing in it treats alcohol poisoning. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** a guest is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or gaps of 10 seconds or more), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Don't leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off," and lay them on their side if they're drowsy. **The morning after, see a doctor if** someone can't keep fluids down for most of the day, has vomit that looks bloody or like coffee grounds, has severe stomach or chest pain, or still feels confused or very unwell more than 24 hours later. Anyone who takes prescription medicine should check with their own doctor or pharmacist before mixing it with alcohol or with anything in a kit.

## Why Wedding Hangover Kits Are a Popular Favor

Traditional favors (engraved coasters, candles, a sugared almond box) often get left on the table. A hangover kit gets used, which is why it has become one of the more popular modern favors and welcome-bag fillers. It also fits the shape of a wedding weekend. Many weddings now run Friday to Sunday with a welcome party, the wedding itself, and a farewell brunch, and the morning after the reception is when guests are checking out of hotels, driving home, or catching flights.

A kit tells guests you thought about that morning. It's also a quiet signal that you want people to look after themselves, and it gives you a natural place to put the practical things guests actually need: the shuttle schedule, the brunch time, and a taxi or rideshare number.

There are three main ways couples use them:

- **As a favor at the reception.** A small bag or box at each place setting or on a table near the exit at the end of the night.
- **In the welcome bag.** Hotel welcome bags for out-of-town guests often include water and snacks already, so a "recovery" pouch fits naturally.
- **As a bathroom basket.** An open basket in the restrooms at the venue with single-serve items guests can take as needed.

Each has its own best contents, which we'll get to after the core list.

## The Core Wedding Hangover Kit Checklist

These items are safe for almost every adult guest, cheap, and genuinely useful. If you only include these, your kit is already better than most.

### 1. Water

Dehydration isn't the whole cause of a hangover, but alcohol does make you lose more fluid than usual, and dry mouth and thirst are some of the most common morning-after complaints. A small bottle of water is the single most useful item in the bag. Custom-labeled mini bottles are a popular wedding touch. If your kit is a reception favor, guests may not open it until they're back at the hotel, which is exactly when it helps.

Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers how much to drink and what works better than plain water when you feel rough.

### 2. Electrolyte packets

Single-serve oral rehydration or electrolyte powders (stick packs that you mix into water) are light, cheap in bulk, and easy to tuck into a small bag. They contain sodium and potassium plus some sugar, which helps the body absorb water. They won't cure a hangover, but they can help if a guest has been sweating on the dance floor or had a stomach upset. Look for packets with a clear ingredient list. Avoid ones heavy on caffeine, because some guests will be sensitive to it and some will be pregnant. Our [electrolyte drinks comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) goes through the main brands.

One note: electrolyte packets with added sugar aren't ideal for guests managing diabetes, so a sugar-free option or a mixed selection in a basket is considerate.

### 3. A salty snack

Pretzels, crackers, or a small bag of salted nuts. Salty, bland carbohydrates are easy on a queasy stomach and help with low energy the next morning. Check for nut allergies before choosing nuts, and if you're not sure, pick pretzels or crackers instead. Individually wrapped, shelf-stable snacks are best, because the kit may sit in a hotel room for a day.

### 4. Something gentle for breakfast

A granola bar, an oat bar, or a small pack of crackers for the morning. Many guests skip breakfast to make checkout or the airport, and eating something helps. For a welcome bag you could add a single-serve instant oatmeal cup or a piece of whole fruit if the bag will be handed out on arrival.

### 5. Ginger chews or mints

Ginger has some research behind it for nausea in general (mostly in pregnancy and motion sickness, not hangovers specifically), and ginger chews are pleasant, small, and safe for most people. Mints or gum help with the "I drank red wine and slept on it" mouth. Our page on [ginger for hangovers](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) explains what's known.

### 6. A note card with the practical details

This is the most underrated item. A small printed card can include:

- A friendly line ("Thanks for dancing all night. Drink this before bed.")
- The brunch time and place, or the shuttle schedule
- A local taxi or rideshare suggestion, and a reminder not to drive after drinking
- If you include any medicine, a short line on how to use it safely (covered below)

That card turns a cute favor into a useful one.

## Optional Add-Ons (and When They Make Sense)

These are nice extras. Include them based on your budget, your crowd, and the setting.

- **Lip balm.** Outdoor and beach weddings dry out lips fast.
- **Sunscreen sachets.** Useful for outdoor weddings or destination weddings in hot climates.
- **Eye mask and earplugs.** Great for a welcome bag, especially if guests are sharing hotel rooms.
- **Hair ties, bobby pins, and blister plasters.** Better for a bathroom basket than a favor, but always appreciated by guests in new shoes.
- **Tissues, wet wipes, or makeup wipes.** Good for a basket.
- **Instant coffee or tea bags.** A thoughtful touch for hotel rooms with a kettle. Decaf or herbal is the kinder default for a crowd.
- **A DHM sample or packet.** Covered in its own section below. Optional, and only with a clear label.

## Painkillers in Wedding Kits: The Rules That Keep Guests Safe

This is the part most "wedding hangover kit" lists skip, and it matters more at a wedding than anywhere else, because you can't know what medications your guests take or what conditions they have.

**You don't have to include a painkiller at all.** Many couples leave medicine out entirely and put the money into better water bottles or snacks. That's a perfectly good choice, especially for a large guest list or a crowd with a wide age range.

If you do include one, follow these rules:

1. **Only sealed, single-dose packets in original packaging.** Travel-size packets of one or two tablets, still sealed with the label and dosing information printed on them. Never pour loose pills into little bags or decorative tins. Unlabeled pills are a safety problem (people don't know what or how much they're taking) and they look bad.
2. **Never more than one dose per kit.** A kit isn't a pharmacy.
3. **Label which drug it is and add an alcohol note.** For example: "For a headache tomorrow morning. Take with food and water. Not before bed or while drinking. Skip if you're pregnant, take blood thinners, or have stomach, kidney or liver problems."
4. **Pick one type and say what it is.** The two common choices each have a trade-off with alcohol:
   - **Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol)** is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver, and alcohol adds to that load. It should never be taken "pre-emptively" while drinking. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver chemistry and safe timing.
   - **Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs** (Advil, Motrin, naproxen, aspirin) are easier on the liver but can irritate the stomach lining, which alcohol has already irritated, and they carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who drink. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers this in more detail.
5. **Check your venue's and hotel's rules.** Some venues or hotels have policies about what can be left in rooms or handed out, and a few destination countries have stricter rules about over-the-counter medicines. Ask your planner or hotel coordinator before you buy in bulk.
6. **Keep kits away from children.** If kids are on the guest list, don't put medicine kits on tables or in bathroom baskets where they can reach them. Hand them out to adults directly or leave them in adult guests' hotel rooms.

The honest summary: a painkiller is the one item in a wedding kit that can cause harm if it's used wrong. A well-labeled single packet is fine for most adult guests. Skipping it entirely is also fine.

## What to Leave Out of a Wedding Hangover Kit

Some items show up on a lot of online lists but don't belong in a kit you're handing to a crowd.

- **Loose or unlabeled pills of any kind.** Covered above.
- **Sleep aids.** Antihistamine sleep aids (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) and melatonin are not good things to hand out to people who have been drinking. Alcohol plus a sedating antihistamine adds up, and you don't know who's about to drive.
- **Anything sold as a hangover "cure."** There is no good evidence that any product cures a hangover. Labels like "hangover cure" or "never get hungover" promise something nothing can deliver, and some guests will read them as permission to drink more.
- **Energy shots or high-caffeine drinks.** Caffeine can make a pounding head and racing heart worse for some people, and mixing caffeine with alcohol can make people feel less drunk than they are. Some guests are pregnant or have heart conditions.
- **Mini bottles of liquor ("hair of the dog").** It's a common joke favor, but more alcohol in the morning only delays the hangover, and it's risky for anyone about to drive home. Leave the jokes for the card.
- **Prescription anti-nausea medicines.** These need a prescription for a reason.
- **Herbal supplements with no label.** If you include any supplement, it should be in sealed packaging with the full ingredient list visible.

## How to Build Kits for Each Format

### Reception favors

Reception favors should be small enough to carry home in a pocket or a clutch. A small muslin bag, a box, or a clear pouch works well. Keep the contents light:

- Mini water bottle (or skip if it won't fit, and give water at the exit instead)
- One or two electrolyte packets
- A small salty snack
- Ginger chews or mints
- The note card

Put them by the exit or hand them out as guests leave, rather than at place settings. They're less likely to be lost or opened by kids, and they arrive when people need them.

### Welcome bags for out-of-town guests

Welcome bags usually go to the hotel at check-in, so they can be bigger and more useful. A good welcome bag might include:

- One or two full-size bottles of water
- Electrolyte packets
- Snacks for the night and a breakfast bar
- Ginger chews and mints
- Eye mask and earplugs
- Lip balm or sunscreen for outdoor or warm-weather weddings
- A local guide card with the weekend schedule, shuttle times, and the brunch location
- Optionally, one labeled single-dose painkiller packet

Ask the hotel how they distribute welcome bags. Most hotels will hand them out at check-in for a small fee or for free if you've booked a room block.

### Bathroom baskets at the venue

A basket in each restroom is a great way to offer things guests can choose for themselves. This is the best place for the things not everyone needs:

- Mints, gum, and ginger chews
- Hair ties, bobby pins, safety pins
- Blister plasters
- Tissues and wipes
- Hand cream and lip balm
- Electrolyte packets

This is not the place for medicine if children will be at the wedding. Keep painkillers out of open baskets or leave them with the planner or a trusted friend who can hand one over on request.

### The farewell brunch table

If you're hosting a brunch the morning after, a small "recovery station" can replace individual kits: a water dispenser, electrolyte packets, a tray of ginger chews, coffee and tea, and hearty food. This is often cheaper than bags for every guest and is used by the people who actually feel rough. Toast, eggs, potatoes, and fruit are all good choices for a hungover crowd.

## Wording the Label and the Note Card

The label is where most of the fun happens. Many couples use a pun and keep the actual message practical. A few ideas:

- "Hangover Survival Kit"
- "For tomorrow morning"
- "Thanks for partying with us"
- "Recovery Kit"
- "You danced, you drank, you deserve this"
- "Open after the last dance"

On the note card, a few practical lines go a long way:

- "Drink the water before bed."
- "Brunch is at 10 at the lobby restaurant."
- "Please don't drive after drinking. Our shuttle runs until midnight, and [local taxi number] is on the back."
- If there's a painkiller: "One dose of [drug name] for a headache tomorrow. Take with food and water, not with alcohol. Skip if you're pregnant or take other medicines."

Keep the tone friendly. Avoid wording that suggests the kit makes heavy drinking safe or prevents a hangover. "Recovery kit" or "survival kit" is fine. "Hangover cure" overpromises.

## Budget Tiers for a Wedding Hangover Kit

Prices vary a lot by where you buy and how many guests you have. These are rough ranges for a single kit, and buying in bulk usually brings the cost down.

**Simple (about $2 to $4 a kit):** a mini water bottle or an electrolyte packet, a salty snack, a few mints or ginger chews, a printed card, and a small bag or box. This covers the basics and works well for large weddings.

**Standard (about $5 to $8 a kit):** everything in the simple kit, plus a second electrolyte packet, a breakfast bar, lip balm, and a nicer pouch or a custom label on the water bottle.

**Deluxe (about $10 to $20 a kit or more):** a full welcome bag with full-size water, a selection of snacks, an eye mask and earplugs, sunscreen, a custom tote, and optionally a labeled single-dose painkiller or a small supplement sample.

Ways to save money:

- **Skip the water in favors and give it at the exit.** A cooler of bottled water by the door does the same job at a fraction of the price per guest.
- **Do kits for the wedding party and out-of-town guests only.** Local guests going home to their own kitchens don't need much.
- **Use a brunch recovery station instead of individual bags.**
- **Buy electrolyte packets and snacks in bulk.** Warehouse stores and multi-packs are much cheaper than single units.
- **Assemble them yourself.** Many couples turn kit assembly into a small pre-wedding gathering with the wedding party.

## The Wedding Party and Couple's Own Kit

Guest kits are one thing. The people who need one most are often the wedding party and the couple, because they've had the longest day, the most toasts, and often the least food.

**For the couple, set aside a "day after" bag** with:

- Two big bottles of water and a few electrolyte packets
- A proper breakfast plan (room service ordered the night before, or a friend bringing breakfast)
- Comfortable clothes and a sleep mask
- Phone chargers, because both phones will be dead
- Any regular medications you take
- A painkiller you know you can take safely

Many couples barely eat at their own reception because they spend the night greeting guests. The single biggest thing you can do to feel better the next morning is to ask your caterer to box up two plates of dinner, and to ask someone to make sure you actually eat them. Our guide on [how not to get drunk at a wedding](/never-hungover/how-not-to-get-drunk-at-a-wedding) covers pacing for guests, the wedding party, and the couple across the whole day.

**For the wedding party,** a shared bag in the getting-ready room with water, snacks, and electrolyte packets is more useful than individual favors. Keep in mind the morning before the wedding matters too. If there was a rehearsal dinner or a late night before, being hungover while getting ready is common. Real food, water, and a little sleep do more than anything in a box.

## Planning for Different Guests

A good wedding kit works for the whole guest list. A few groups to think about:

- **Guests who don't drink.** Plenty of your guests won't be drinking, for health, religion, pregnancy, recovery, or simple preference. Calling the kit a "recovery kit" or "morning-after kit" rather than a "hangover kit" keeps it welcoming, and most of the contents (water, snacks, lip balm) are useful to everyone anyway.
- **Pregnant guests.** Electrolyte packets, crackers, and ginger chews are generally fine. Supplements, painkillers, and caffeine products are not things to hand to a pregnant guest without her own doctor's advice. A clear label lets her skip them.
- **Older guests.** Older adults are more likely to take daily medicines like blood thinners or blood pressure pills, which interact with alcohol and with painkillers. Another reason the label matters.
- **Guests under 21 (or under the local drinking age).** A hangover kit with a cute drinking pun is a mixed message for teenagers. If your guest list includes them, give the favors to adults directly.
- **Guests with allergies or dietary needs.** Check snacks for nuts, gluten, and other common allergens, or include a mix.

## Destination Weddings: What Changes

Destination weddings bring their own morning-after problems: heat, sun, unfamiliar food, and travel days.

- **Hot climates and beach weddings.** Add sunscreen, lip balm with SPF, and more electrolyte packets. Heat and alcohol together raise the risk of dehydration and heat exhaustion. Remind guests to drink water during the day, not just after the reception. Our [Mexico travel hangover guide](/never-hungover/ultimate-mexico-travel-hangover-prevention-guide-2025) has more on drinking in the heat.
- **Bottled water.** In places where tap water isn't safe to drink, bottled water in the welcome bag is a real health item, not a decoration.
- **Customs and local rules.** Some countries restrict bringing in certain over-the-counter medicines or supplements, and rules differ from country to country. If you're shipping or packing supplies, check the destination's customs rules first, or buy locally.
- **Travel days.** Many guests fly home the day after. A kit that helps them feel well enough to travel (water, snacks, a sleep mask) is ideal.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Some couples include a DHM supplement packet in welcome bags or keep it in their own kit.

Here's what we know. Most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how alcohol acts on the brain and how the liver processes it. Human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers reliably in people. It doesn't change how much alcohol is in your blood in any way you can count on, and it doesn't make drinking more safe for driving. Some people find it helpful; others notice no difference.

If you want to include DHM:

- **It's better suited to the wedding party or the couple's own kit than to 150 guest favors.** You can talk to the people you're giving it to and they can decide.
- **Label it clearly.** Full ingredient list, the dose, and a line like "a supplement some people take with drinking; skip if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or take prescription medicine."
- **Use sealed, retail packaging.** Never repackage capsules.

Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much and when people typically take it, and our [medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains who should check with a doctor first. If you want to try it for yourself before the wedding, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget pick with plenty of servings for a wedding party, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which comes in individual servings. Our roundup of the [best DHM supplements](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) compares more options. Whatever you choose, it's an extra, not a substitute for water, food, and pacing.

## What Matters More Than the Kit

A kit helps the morning after. What happens during the reception matters much more:

- **Feed people well and early.** Passed appetizers during cocktail hour and dinner served on time do more for your guests' mornings than any favor. A late-night snack (pizza, sliders, fries) near the end of the reception is a crowd favorite for a reason.
- **Make water easy.** Water on every table and a water station by the bar and dance floor.
- **Offer good non-alcoholic drinks.** A signature mocktail or quality non-alcoholic options make it easy for guests to pace or skip a round.
- **Plan the ride home.** A shuttle to the hotel, a taxi list, or rideshare codes. Drunk driving after weddings is a real risk, and a ride plan prevents it in a way no kit can.
- **Close the bar before the last dance.** Many venues stop serving 30 minutes to an hour before the end, which gives people a little time before they leave.
- **Brief a friend or two.** Ask a trusted, sober-ish friend or the planner to keep an eye out for anyone who's had far too much, and to know the emergency signs in the box at the top of this page.

If you're worried that the line between a bad hangover and something more serious is blurry, our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to look for. The short rule: if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, is vomiting while drowsy, or has a seizure, call 911 and don't wait.

## A Simple Wedding Hangover Kit Packing List

Copy this list for your planning:

**Every kit (favor or welcome bag):**
- Mini or full bottle of water
- 1 to 2 electrolyte packets
- Salty snack (pretzels or crackers)
- Breakfast bar
- Ginger chews or mints
- Note card with brunch time, shuttle, and a reminder not to drive

**Welcome bag extras:**
- Eye mask and earplugs
- Lip balm and sunscreen (outdoor or warm weather)
- Local guide and weekend schedule
- Optional: one sealed, labeled single-dose painkiller

**Bathroom basket:**
- Mints, gum, ginger chews
- Hair ties, bobby pins, safety pins, blister plasters
- Tissues and wipes
- Electrolyte packets

**Couple's day-after bag:**
- Water and electrolytes
- Boxed reception dinner plus a breakfast plan
- Comfortable clothes and chargers
- Regular medications and a painkiller you know is safe for you

**Leave out:** loose pills, sleep aids, energy shots, liquor minis, and anything labeled as a hangover cure.

If you're planning a bachelorette or bachelor weekend too, our [bachelorette hangover kit guide](/never-hungover/bachelorette-hangover-kit) covers multi-day kits, and our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) page has basic and deluxe kits for any occasion.

## The Bottom Line

A wedding hangover kit is a thoughtful, useful favor when you keep it simple: water, electrolytes, a salty snack, something for breakfast, ginger or mints, and a card with the practical details. Medicine is optional and needs sealed, single-dose packaging with a clear alcohol note, or you can leave it out. Plan for the whole guest list, including people who don't drink, are pregnant, or take daily medicines. And remember that good food, easy water, and a safe ride home do more for your guests' mornings than anything in the bag.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What do you put in a wedding hangover kit?**

The essentials are a bottle of water, one or two electrolyte packets, a salty snack like pretzels, a breakfast bar, ginger chews or mints, and a note card with the brunch time and ride home details. Optional extras include lip balm, sunscreen, an eye mask, and earplugs. A painkiller is optional and should only be a sealed, labeled single-dose packet.

**Is it OK to put painkillers in wedding favors?**

It can be, if you're careful. Use only sealed single-dose packets in original packaging, include one dose per kit, and add a note explaining what it is, to take it with food and water the next morning (not while drinking), and to skip it if pregnant or on other medicines. Keep medicine kits away from children, and check venue and hotel rules. Leaving painkillers out entirely is also a perfectly good choice.

**How much does a wedding hangover kit cost per guest?**

Roughly $2 to $4 for a simple kit, $5 to $8 for a standard kit, and $10 to $20 or more for a deluxe welcome bag, depending on what you include and where you buy. Buying in bulk, skipping water in favors, or offering a brunch recovery station instead of individual bags can bring costs down.

**When should you give out wedding hangover kits?**

As guests leave the reception is the most practical time, because they get the kit right when they need it and it's less likely to get lost or opened by kids. For out-of-town guests, a welcome bag delivered to their hotel at check-in works well. A bathroom basket can be available all night.

**What should a wedding hangover kit label say?**

Something friendly like "Hangover Survival Kit," "Recovery Kit," or "Open after the last dance," plus practical details on the card: brunch time, shuttle schedule, a ride home reminder, and safe-use instructions for any medicine. Avoid calling it a "hangover cure," because nothing can promise that.

**Can I include DHM in wedding hangover kits?**

You can, but it's better suited to the wedding party or your own kit than to every guest. There is no good evidence that DHM reliably prevents hangovers in people, and most of the research is from animal studies. If you include it, use sealed retail packaging with the full ingredient list and a note that guests who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or on prescription medicines should skip it.

**What should the couple pack for the day after the wedding?**

Water and electrolyte packets, a boxed plate of the reception dinner and a breakfast plan, comfortable clothes, phone chargers, regular medications, and a painkiller you know is safe for you. Many couples barely eat at their own reception, so arranging food for the night and the morning is the single most helpful step.

**How do I make a hangover kit inclusive for guests who don't drink?**

Call it a "recovery kit" or "morning-after kit" instead of a hangover kit, and fill it mostly with things everyone can use: water, snacks, mints, lip balm, and an eye mask. Label any painkiller or supplement clearly so pregnant guests or those on medication can skip it.
